C. Minardi

M. Ippoliti 
Electrophysiological 
evaluation 
of the stiff-man syndrome: 
further data 
Received: 3 October 1995 
Accepted: 21 January 1996 
Sirs: We read with interest the paper 
by Meink et al. [18] concerning the 
neurophysiological evaluation of the 
stiff-man syndrome (SMS). The au- 
thors found in SMS a peculiar form 
of myoclonic jerking, termed spas- 
modic reflex myoclonus, as well as 
abnormalities of segmental and 
suprasegmental reflex organization. 
They speculated that the stiffness of 
SMS is a fragment of spasms, hy- 
pothesizing, as a common neuronal 
mechanism, a dysfunction of the in- 
terneurons of the spinal grey matter. 
These data have prompted us to re- 
port the neurophysiological study of 
a new case of SMS. To our knowl- 
edge, two of the reflex activities ex- 
amined have not previously been 
evaluated in SMS. 
A 63-year-old farmer complained, 
from the age of 48 years, of episodic 
stiffness of lumbar axial muscles cul- 
minating in painful spasms of the 
lower right limb, triggered by emo- 
tional stimuli. From the age of 50 the 
stiffness spread to the controlateral 
lower limb, truncal, upper limb and 
neck muscles, hindering voluntary 
movements; painful spasms wors- 
ened in frequency, intensity and du- 
ration triggered also by mechanical 
and sensory stimuli. 
Neurological evaluation showed 
no abnormalities in the short-lasting 
inter-spasm periods, but gentle skin 
stimulation, a sudden noise, or an 
emotional input triggered a diffuse 
painful muscular spasm. During the 
spasm the spinal hyperlordosis wors- 
ened, and the patient's voluntary 
movements were severely limited; he 
assumed a "wooden soldier" appear- 
ance. Neuropsychological assess- 
ment was normal. 
The administration of 35 mg/day 
diazepam reduced the spasms; 
plasma exchange followed by steroid 
administration permitted us to taper 
the dose of diazepam to 5 mg/day. 
Extensive laboratory evaluation 
revealed normal values except for 
positive antibodies directed against 
glutamic acid decarboxylase in the 
serum. Brain CT and MRI were nor- 
mal. Needle EMG examination of a 
pair of antagonistic muscles (quadri- 
ceps and biceps femoris, tibialis an- 
terior and soleus) revealed a "sponta- 
neous" activity composed of normal 
motor unit action potentials firing 
asynchronously. A full recruitment 
pattern of 2.5-3 mV amplitude dur- 
ing maximal effort was observed. 
However, it provoked diffusion of 
the contraction to the ipsilateral and 
contralateral muscles. With a tactile, 
acoustic or emotional stimulus, the 
contraction increased markedly and 
became painful, while the adminis- 
tration of 10 mg diazepam i.v. abol- 
ished both the spontaneous activity 
and the effects of exteroceptive stim- 
uli. Motor and sensory nerve con- 
duction evaluation of four nerves 
(right median and peroneal, left ulnar 
and tibial) disclosed normal conduc- 
tion values for the patient's age. 
The silent period was determined 
in the tibialis anterior muscle during 
a voluntary contraction stimulating 
the peroneal nerve at the head of the 
fibula by an electrical shock of 0.1 
ms duration. An H reflex with a nor- 
mal latency was obtained from the 
soleus muscle. The H-M recruitment 
curve showed a normal shape, as did 
the H-H recovery curve by paired 
shock [conditioning stimulus 0.8 of 
the motor threshold (MT) test stimu- 
lus = Hmax/2]. The H/M ratio was 
normal, i.e. 0.45.

RII and RIII of the short head of the 
biceps femoris muscle [8] and exten- 
sion (RPPS) of the soleus [15] were

Our observation fulfils both the 
clinical as well as the electrophysio- 
logical criteria of SMS. In fact, the 
stiffness and rigidity began in axial 
muscles, slowly involving the proxi- 
mal limb muscles; the painful 
spasms were triggered by sudden 
noise, movement or emotional upset; 
the neurological and intellective 
functions were normal; no abnormal- 
ities were disclosed by neuroradio- 
logical investigations [ 11]. EMG ex- 
amination showed the constantly 
found electrophysiological counter- 
part of this syndrome, i.e. the sponta- 
neous firing of motor unit action po- 
tentials involving antagonistic mus- 
cles, culminating in spasm induced 
by the above causes. The excessive 
motor outflow led us to investigate 
the function of different spinal struc- 
tures to understand better the patho- 
physiology of this peculiar kind of 
impaired motor control. 
Evaluation of the H/M ratio in the 
present case disclosed normal values. 
This ratio was found to be increased 
two of five patients in the series of 
Meinck et al. [18] and in the two 
cases of Mamoli et al. [12], but was 
within normal limits in another six 
cases of SMS [3, 14, 20]. A comple- 
mentary technique, the evaluation of 
the F wave, to evaluate the central 
drive acting on motor neurons gave 
equivocal data. In the study of 
Meinck et al. [ 16] an increase in F 
wave amplitude was found, while the 
excitability coefficient value was in 
the normal range in the four SMS 
patients evaluated by Correale et al. 
[3]. It can be inferred that at present 
we have more evidence against than 
in favour of a primary hyperex- 
citability of the motor neurons in 
SMS. Consequently, the systems 
modulating the motor outflow need 
to be evaluated. 
Vibratory inhibition was clearly 
impaired in our case, in agreement 
with the data of Meinck et al. [18]. 
Three previous reports concerning 
cases of SMS [10, 14, 20] also noted 
defective vibratory inhibition, further 
supporting the hypothesis that the 
GABAergic presynaptic inhibition is 
defective in SMS [18]. 
Evaluation of polysynaptic non- 
nociceptive flexion (RID or exten- 
sion (RPPS) reflex activities showed, 
in our case, a clear defect of habitua- 
tion. In addition, an abnormal diffu- 
sion of the reflex activity to the an- 
tagonistic muscle was recorded. Both 
these abnormalities have been found 
in two other cases of SMS [10, 14], 
indicating an impaired segmental re- 
flex control, tentatively located in 
the interneuronal chains. It is inter- 
esting to note that with a different 
technique, Meinck and co-workers 
[18] found an abnormal reflex pat- 
tern of the tibialis anterior polysy- 
naptic reflex with abnormal temporal 
facilitation, considered to be due to 
impaired control of segmental mech- 
anisms. Meinck et al. [18] noted the 
similarity of the reflex activity pat- 
tern with that observed in spasticity, 
contrasting it with the lack of pyra-

midal symptoms and normal cortico- 
muscular latencies found in SMS pa- 
tients [17]. The absence of pyramidal 
involvement in SMS, in spite of an 
abnormal polysynaptic spinal reflex 
activity pattern, was confirmed in the 
present case by the normal Ia recip- 
rocal inhibition activity of the H re- 
flex. In fact, in patients with an up- 
per motor neuron syndrome the reci- 
procal Ia inhibition is reduced [5]. If 
confirmed in other SMS cases, this 
can be considered additional proof 
that the SMS deranged spinal reflex 
organization shares some, but not all, 
features found in spasticity. 
A normal silent period has con- 
stantly been found, as in the present 
case, in the eight cases of SMS eval- 
uated with this technique [3, 10, 12. 
18]. 
Several physiological mechanisms 
are involved in the generation of 
spasticity, among others (for a re- 
view see [9]) the Renshaw cell cir- 
cuitry. The hypothesis of preserved 
function of Renshaw cells in SMS 
seems to be confirmed by the normal 
data obtained in the only specific 
evaluation of this circuitry available 
in SMS [2]. 
In our case, we tested the behav- 
iour of the Ib autogenic inhibition 
[19]. The normal inhibition was re- 
placed by a facilitation in the inter- 
stimulus delay of 1-6 ms. Impair- 
ment of Ib autogenic inhibition has 
been found in spasticity as well as in 
rigidity [5]. It is interesting to note 
that a linear correlation was found 
between Ib test abnormalities and the 
degree of stiffness [5]. This func- 
tional compartment has not been 
evaluated before in SMS and further 
evaluations are needed. However, it 
not unexpected to find this compart- 
ment impaired in a disease in which 
enhanced tone represents a major 
feature. 
On the basis of the long loop re- 
flexes to the hand muscles in three 
SMS cases, Meinck et al. [18] sug- 
gested a disturbed transcortical reflex 
mediation, thus implying a central 
derangement of spinal control in 
SMS. In favour of supraspinal struc- 
ture involvement we can consider, 
additional to the electrophysiological 
evidence, the disruption of the nor- 
mal sleep pattern. With the exception 
of one observation [20], the sleep 
pattern was altered in all SMS cases 
examined (present report; [1, 6, 7, 
14]). Moreover, polysomnographic 
studies have constantly disclosed ad- 
ditional motor abnormalities in SMS

553 
sleep, consisting of an excess of my- 
oclonic jerks, paroxysmal spasms, or 
nocturnal myoclonus, all events con- 
sistent with a derangement of 
supraspinal structures [ 13]. 
In conclusion, a derangement of 
supraspinal structures involved in 
motor control and a defective spinal 
motor outflow, probably due to an 
impaired pre-motor activity of in- 
terneural chains, are currently impli- 
cated in SMS. It is worth noting that 
different electrophysiological tech- 
niques exploring different peripheral 
or central compartments point to the 
same conclusions.

Symptomatic palatal tremor 
is associated with signs 
of cerebellar dysfunction 
Received: 20 November 1995 
Accepted: 3 February 1996 
Sirs: Symptomatic palatal tremor 
(SPT) is clinically characterized by 
rhythmic, slow-frequency movements 
of the soft palate, often combined 
with time-locked movements of ad- 
ditional branchial or extremity mus- 
cles [4, 6]. It has been known for a 
long time that SPT is commonly ac- 
companied by a unique abnormality 
of the inferior olive, called hyper- 
trophic degeneration (HD). Indeed, 
all but one of the 44 autopsied SPT 
cases reported so far showed HD [2]. 
Mainly French neurologists have 
demonstrated (references in [6]) that 
HD of the inferior olive develops fol- 
lowing a lesion within the Guillain- 
Mollm'et triangle along a pathway 
from the cerebellar nuclei through 
the upper cerebellar peduncle, pass- 
ing the contralateral red nucleus 
without relay and descending within 
the central tegmental tract to the in- 
ferior olive [6]. 
Besides rhythmic palatal move- 
ments, the clinical symptoms of SPT 
include clinical signs of brain-stem 
and cerebellar dysfunction [4, 6]. 
These have been commonly assigned 
to a lesion which was assumed to af- 
fect the cerebellum, on the one hand, 
and the Guillain-Mollaret triangle, on 
the other [6]. However, earlier patho-

SMS. In favour of supraspinal struc- 
ture involvement we can consider, 
additional to the electrophysiological 
evidence, the disruption of the nor- 
mal sleep pattern. With the exception 
of one observation [20], the sleep 
pattern was altered in all SMS cases 
examined (present report; [1, 6, 7, 
14]). Moreover, polysomnographic 
studies have constantly disclosed ad- 
ditional motor abnormalities in SMS

sleep, consisting of an excess of my- 
oclonic jerks, paroxysmal spasms, or 
nocturnal myoclonus, all events con- 
sistent with a derangement of 
supraspinal structures [ 13]. 
In conclusion, a derangement of 
supraspinal structures involved in 
motor control and a defective spinal 
motor outflow, probably due to an 
impaired pre-motor activity of in- 
terneural chains, are currently impli- 
cated in SMS. It is worth noting that 
different electrophysiological tech- 
niques exploring different peripheral 
or central compartments point to the 
same conclusions.
